model.label: Compulsory social health insurance with a single national fund (CNS), financed by income-based contributions shared by employers and employees plus a fixed State share from general taxes; mostly fee-for-service with upfront payment and reimbursement, now increasingly paid directly through the PID scheme

overview.statement: Luxembourg has compulsory social health insurance managed by the National Health Fund (Caisse Nationale de Santé, CNS), which also runs long-term care insurance.
Governance sits with the Ministry of Health and Social Security and its Health Directorate; the ministry plans hospital infrastructure and services but has no legal power to plan outpatient care.
The CNS negotiates agreements with providers in both hospital and outpatient care, and these agreements bind any provider delivering services covered by the insurance.

Licensed professionals whose association has a framework agreement with the CNS are contracted automatically and must follow CNS tariffs and reimbursement rules; professions outside that list, such as osteopaths, cannot bill the insurance.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

overview.statement: There is no gatekeeping: patients choose their providers freely, although some initiatives have tried to make the general practitioner the usual first point of contact.
The Ministry of Health and Social Security, formed by merging the former health and social security ministries, is responsible for health care planning, legislation and financing.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

financing.statement: The health insurance scheme is paid for by contributions shared between the State, employers and employees, and membership is compulsory for everyone who works or receives a replacement income.

Social security contributions from employers, employees, pensioners and pension funds supply around 60% of public health financing; the other 40% is a fixed State transfer paid out of general tax revenue.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services?

financing.statement: General tax revenue pays a fixed State share equal to 40% of health insurance contributions and 40% of long-term care insurance spending, and also funds public health programmes and infrastructure investment.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The health insurance contribution rate has been 5.6% of gross income since 2014; people entitled to cash sickness and maternity benefits from the CNS pay an extra 0.5%.
Employers and employees generally split the contribution equally; the self-employed and voluntarily insured people pay all of their own contributions.
Contributions rise in proportion to income, do not depend on health risk, and dependants covered through a family member pay nothing.

From 1 June 2026 the ceiling on contributory earnings for all schemes except long-term care insurance was EUR 13,856.63, and the monthly social minimum wage, which is the minimum contribution base for unskilled workers aged 18 and over, was EUR 2,771.33.
Long-term care insurance is funded by a separate 1.4% contribution levied on gross income, asset income and replacement income, with no employer share.
Government health schemes are mostly paid from non-earmarked taxes; the one earmarked tax, on electricity, goes to long-term care insurance but supplied only 0.2% of its revenue in 2022.

The health and maternity insurance had EUR 4,776.9 million of current revenue in 2025: EUR 2,805.2 million in contributions, EUR 1,870.1 million in flat-rate State contributions, EUR 20.7 million in other State contributions and EUR 81.0 million in other revenue.

locator.table: Tableau 1 - Équilibre financier de l'AMM (columns 2024 and 2025 are final accounts)

financing.statement: Government and compulsory insurance schemes paid 85% of current health spending (EU average 80%) and voluntary health insurance premiums 4.4%; household out-of-pocket payments were 10% of spending in 2023 (EU average 16%).
In 2022, compulsory health insurance financed 78.7% of current health expenditure and other government schemes 7.4%, making up a public share of 86.1%.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The Ministry of Health and Social Security pays contributions for people who are not covered as dependants, such as some children, students or disabled people, and the Ministry of Family Affairs pays them for social welfare recipients.
People who join the health insurance voluntarily paid 5.6% of the monthly minimum wage in 2024, or EUR 143.97 a month.
Voluntary health insurance financed only 4.1% of current health spending in 2022, but 67.3% of the resident population bought complementary private cover that year.
The CMCM cannot refuse cover to anyone insured by a statutory fund in Luxembourg or by statutory health insurance in a bordering country, and may not require medical records for admission.
Commercial private health insurers are supervised by the Insurance Commission under the Ministry of Finance and set admission and premiums on the basis of risk assessment.
Employees' compulsory health and pension insurance contributions are deductible from taxable income without limit.
Household out-of-pocket payments were 8.7% of current health spending in 2022, but the review notes this is probably an underestimate because such spending is not collected systematically.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: By law the CNS's board resets the contribution rate from 1 January when the budget shows the reserve outside its legal limits; if the board has not acted by 1 December, the social security minister sets the rate.

locator.section: Évolution de la situation financière et perspective pour 2027

covered.statement: Membership is compulsory for anyone who is economically active, under 18, or receiving State benefits or replacement income (such as sickness pay, unemployment benefit or a pension).

Social health insurance covered 92.6% of the resident population in 2023; about 36% of everyone it covered were cross-border workers living in Belgium, France or Germany, and employees of international organisations (11,900 people in 2022) and their dependants are exempt.

All members and their dependants receive the same benefits whatever their status, health risk, contributions or length of insurance; the package covers medical and dental care, other health professionals including psychotherapists, hospital care, laboratory tests, imaging, medicines, medical devices, psychiatric and geriatric rehabilitation, patient transport, palliative care and some preventive services.

Not covered are non-prescribed goods and services, anything outside the national fee schedules, charges above official tariffs and long-term care below 3.5 hours a week; some reimbursements are limited by age or condition and need prior approval from the social security medical control body (CMSS).
Employers keep paying wages during sickness, typically for 77 days, before the CNS takes over sickness cash benefits; CNS maternity benefits cover 8 weeks before and 12 weeks after birth.

The ministry can change the national fee schedules, which define reimbursed services and tariffs, on the advice of a Nomenclature Commission whose members are appointed by the ministry, the CNS board and doctors' representatives, and which decides by majority vote.
There is no formal health technology assessment agency; the CMSS gives binding advice on adding new medicines to the outpatient reimbursement list after manufacturers apply.

Each year the ministry convenes a 'quadripartite' committee of government, employee, employer and provider representatives to review the insurance's finances and propose efficiency measures; it advises but cannot decide.

A new dental fee schedule took effect in 2024, replacing an outdated one whose low tariffs ignored newer techniques and which dentists had offset by extra billing; dental care for under-18s has been fully covered since 2013.

Some specialised treatments are offered only at one national site or abroad; care involving specialised equipment, hospital infrastructure or an overnight stay requires authorisation, which the CNS can refuse if treatment is possible in Luxembourg within a medically justifiable time.

cost_sharing.statement: Insured people typically get 88% of the official fee back for medical and dental services, and a fixed charge, rather than a percentage, applies only to adults' hospital stays.
From 1 June 2026 inpatients pay EUR 26.79 per day in hospital and day-hospital patients EUR 13.40 per day, and dental care is reimbursed in full up to EUR 83.88 a year.

For outpatient doctors, coinsurance is 20% for GP visits and 12% for medical acts; children, pregnancy-related care, cancer care and preventive and screening exams are exempt, and statutory charges are capped at 2.5% of the previous year's contributory income, a cap that does not apply to charges above the official tariff.

locator.table: Table 3.3 User charges for health services: ambulatory primary and specialist care

cost_sharing.statement: Medicines are normally reimbursed at 80%, those of moderate therapeutic benefit at 40%, and those vital for particularly serious or chronic conditions at 100%.

In 2023 the statutory insurance paid 67% of retail pharmaceutical spending, voluntary insurance 3% and patients 30%; patients' share was higher than in Belgium, France and Germany but below the EU average of 36%.
Daily hospital co-payments are limited to 30 days or EUR 765 a year, and children under 18 and women in the first 12 days after giving birth are exempt.

locator.table: Table 3.3 User charges for health services: inpatient stay

cost_sharing.statement: Patients usually pay the official tariff up front and claim reimbursement from the CNS afterwards; laboratory tests, hospital stays, medicines, physiotherapy and long-term care are instead billed directly, so the patient pays only the statutory share.
A direct-payment scheme (paiement immédiat direct, PID) introduced in 2023 lets the CNS pay providers at the point of care instead of the patient paying and claiming back.

By July 2025 about 1,900 of the 2,321 registered active doctors had joined PID and around 75% of services were paid through it; the largest hospital joined in January 2025, and from January 2026 all doctors must be equipped for electronic billing.

On top of official tariffs, doctors may charge 'personal convenience' fees, for example for a first-class or single room, where the tariff can be 66% higher; the extra fee has no set level and must only be fixed 'with tact and moderation'.

CNS billing data for 2021 put average patient cost-sharing on outpatient services, including surcharges, at 16.2% of the insurance's cost, with the highest shares for visual aids (72.9%) and dental services (37.1%).

Since 2013 a 'social third-party payment' (TPS) lets low-income people get outpatient care without paying up front, using a time-limited certificate from the local social welfare office, which decides case by case with no national eligibility rule.
Use of the social third-party payment rose from 4,757 insured people in 2018 to 6,226 in 2022, about 0.6% of insurance beneficiaries each year.

financial_hardship.statement: Medical products made up around 60% of out-of-pocket payments among households with catastrophic health spending in 2017.
Cost-sharing for basic dentures, hearing aids and optical care often requires complementary private insurance, which low-income households find hard to afford or which covers them only partly.
The government names illness, alongside job loss and divorce, among the life events that often destabilise household finances and lead to over-indebtedness.

locator.section: Une réalité qui peut toucher tout le monde

financial_hardship.statement: New applications to enter the over-indebtedness procedure stayed fairly stable despite recent crises: 60 in 2022, 52 in 2023 and 51 in 2024.

additional_care.statement: Long-term care insurance, introduced in 1998, covers help with essential daily activities such as washing, eating, dressing and moving, plus assistive technology and home adaptations; it also pays informal carers' pension contributions and offers them training.
Long-term care services themselves are fully covered; the 20% of household out-of-pocket spending that went on long-term care in 2022 was for accommodation and meals in care facilities.

Dental care accounted for nearly a fifth of out-of-pocket payments in 2022, and the dental sector has no supervisory body, so regulatory breaches, for example in advertising, often go undetected or without legal consequences.

access.statement: In 2024 only 1.9% of people who needed medical care reported unmet needs, against an EU average of 3.6%; among people at risk of poverty the rate was 2.5%, against 6.0% across the EU.
Unmet need for dental care was 3.1% of those needing it in 2024 (EU average 6.3%); among people at risk of poverty it was 7.7%, about half the EU rate of 13.6%.

Despite compulsory insurance, at least 1,182 people lacked coverage in 2021, mainly people without an official address or declared work, who often cannot open a bank account and so cannot join the CNS.

A universal coverage pilot (CUSS) started in 2022 pays insurance premiums and cost-sharing for residents who cannot otherwise join the insurance and funds social workers to support them; about 300 people were enrolled by February 2025, and the government planned to extend it depending on an evaluation due at the end of 2025.

Because the population is small, some specialised services are not available and patients often have to be treated abroad; waiting times for emergency, specialist, diagnostic and cancer care remain a public concern.

Most mammograms, MRI and CT scans in 2022-2023 were completed within two months, with MRI waits stabilised by extended opening hours, and the National Health Laboratory cut waits for biopsy results from 19 days in 2024 to 8 days in 2025.

Waits for diagnostics still vary between hospitals and demand from non-residents is high, while the rate of diagnostic exams per person is above the EU average, raising concern about low-value care that audits are addressing.
Luxembourg had 4.0 physicians per 1,000 people in 2023, slightly below the EU average of 4.3, because it long had no full medical training of its own and has relied on doctors trained abroad.
Nurse density was 14.2 per 1,000 people in 2023, well above the EU average of 8.5, though many nurses were trained abroad.
Some 900 nursing posts need filling over the next five years, far more than domestic training can supply: it produced 68 nursing graduates in 2023-24.
The share of hospital employees who commute from neighbouring countries rose from 44.9% in 2019 to 48% in 2023.
A 2019 workforce report projected that 59% to 69% of medical doctors would retire by 2034.

In the OECD Patient-Reported Indicator Survey (PaRIS), 93% of primary care patients rated the care they got as very good (86% across 10 EU countries) and 91% felt involved in decisions, but only 56% felt confident managing their own care (EU 63%).
Patients often do not know what they will be charged, including up-front payments and cost-sharing, until the consultation or treatment is over.
About 85.5% of people helped by Médecins du Monde Luxembourg in 2021 reported that money problems were a major barrier to getting care.

locator.section: Box 2 What are the key gaps in coverage?

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth reached 83.5 years in 2024, almost two years above the EU average; women lived 4.7 years longer than men, a smaller gap than the EU average of 5.2 years.
Preventable mortality fell 21% between 2012 and 2022, to 120 deaths per 100,000 people against an EU average of 168, one of the lowest rates in the EU.
Adjusted for age, Luxembourg's treatable mortality of 60.3 deaths per 100,000 in 2020 was the EU's second lowest, and its preventable mortality (133.7 per 100,000) was also among the lowest.

Admissions for asthma, COPD, congestive heart failure and diabetes, conditions usually manageable outside hospital, totalled 553 per 100,000 people in 2023 for the selection measured, above the EU average of 513.

Colorectal cancer screening reached only 25% of people aged 55-74 in 2023 (EU 48%); cervical screening, done opportunistically without a national programme, was 62% (EU 58%) but has been declining since before the pandemic.
Luxembourg's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 87.5 (85.6-89.0) in 2019, 19.6 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: Healthy life years at birth in 2021 were below the EU average for both women (61.6 vs 64.2) and men (62.3 vs 63.1).
A quarter of all deaths in 2021 were attributable to behavioural risks such as smoking, poor diet, alcohol and physical inactivity.
Adult obesity rose from 16% in 2017 to 17% in 2022, above the EU average of 15%, and overweight or obesity among adolescents climbed from 18% in 2014 to 22% in 2022.

costs.statement: Health spending was EUR 4,614 per person in 2023, 20% above the EU average of EUR 3,832.

Health spending as a share of GDP is not a fully representative measure: GDP includes the economic activity of cross-border workers, while health spending data leave out their care, most of which happens in their home countries.

Health accounts data exclude care given to non-residents, who made up 30% of the insured population and accounted for one sixth of insurance health care spending, which may distort the overall picture.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

costs.statement: Outpatient care took the largest share of health spending in 2023 (33%, EU 28%), followed by inpatient care (27%) and long-term care (18%), while pharmaceuticals and medical devices took 14% (EU 18%).
Prevention's share of health spending dropped from 7% in 2021, during the pandemic, to 3% in 2023, below the EU average of 4% though above the 2% of 2015.
Luxembourg performed 360 CT and MRI scans per 1,000 people in 2021, against an OECD average of 249; only the United States and Korea (362) performed more.
Generics made up only 26% of reimbursed medicines in 2023 (28% in 2024), against an average of 51% across 18 EU countries.

A simulation study projects that rising health care spending per person will be driven mainly by the cost of producing services, while rising long-term care spending will mainly reflect population ageing.
Current spending rose 7.2% in 2025, reflecting an 8.0% rise in spending on benefits in kind (health care) and a 2.5% rise in cash benefits.

Spending on medicines dispensed by hospital pharmacies to outpatients rose 59% between 2020 and 2024, which the profile links to new expensive treatments such as hepatitis C drugs, immunotherapy and chemotherapy.

what_works.statement: Out-of-pocket payments were among the lowest in the EU: 10% of health spending in 2023 (EU 16%) and 1.8% of final household consumption (EU 3.1%).

Free choice of health professionals, with no access restrictions or financial penalties for choosing a doctor, is seen as a key strength of primary care because patients can use a broad range of services, including specialists.

Several safeguards protect people from catastrophic spending: the social third-party payment, an annual cap on official user charges that applies to everyone, and exemptions for groups such as children under 18 and pregnant women for pregnancy-related care.
Day-case surgery rose from 41.6% of hospital admissions in 2017 to 48.1% in 2021.

The profile attributes below-EU-average cancer incidence and mortality to measures such as smoking bans, the population breast screening programme and the National Cancer Plan 2020-24, extended to 2026.
For medicines approved by the EU in 2020-2023, the average wait from EU authorisation to reimbursement in Luxembourg was 449 days, against an EU average of 578 days.

The 2010 reform introduced the social third-party payment, an overall budget for hospital spending and generic substitution, raised cost-sharing and contribution rates (from 5.4% to 5.6%) and increased State funding to 40%; together these measures helped balance the insurance budget.

problems.statement: The health and maternity insurance is expected to run an operating deficit of EUR 133.3 million in 2026 and EUR 189.6 million in 2027, when its reserve would fall to 9.2% of current spending, below the 10% legal minimum.

locator.section: Évolution de la situation financière et perspective pour 2027

problems.statement: To balance the 2027 budget, the health care contribution rate would need to rise from 5.6% to 5.85%.

locator.section: Évolution de la situation financière et perspective pour 2027

problems.statement: There is no mechanism for setting priorities in budget allocation, evidence on cost-effectiveness is little used, and resources are not allocated on a risk-adjusted basis; the review links this to years of healthy insurance finances, and notes underdeveloped prevention and overuse of some care.

Apart from some programmes such as breast cancer screening and specific procedures, prevention is not part of the insurance benefit package, so providers lack incentives to discuss healthy behaviour with patients or encourage regular check-ups.

The exemption for people whose cost-sharing exceeds 2.5% of income is not applied automatically and is poorly publicised: in 2021 about 6,000 people applied, 1,900 qualified and received on average EUR 503, and the CNS cannot tell how many people are entitled.
Some practitioners refuse to treat patients who use the social third-party payment.
There is no national quality assurance programme for health care; monitoring quality is left to providers, and quality data remain insufficient.
Providers use IT systems that cannot talk to each other, so data are recorded inconsistently and medical information is still exchanged largely on paper.
Just over a fifth of residents (22%) had looked at their electronic health record in 2024, slightly below the EU average.
Luxembourg had the highest polypharmacy rate among older adults of 16 countries compared: over 80% of people aged 75 and over took five or more medicines at once in 2019.

Health policy making remains fragmented, partly because there is no comprehensive public health law defining roles and funding, and there is no central body or inter-ministerial committee to align policy across sectors.
Enrolment in the CUSS pilot runs through a few associations and requires intensive monthly social follow-up, which has saturated some of them and in practice limited access for new beneficiaries.

locator.section: Exposé des motifs: Projet pilote de la CUSS

problems.statement: The hospital payment system does not reward efficiency: hospital financing is resource-based rather than results-based, physicians' services are reimbursed separately from the hospital framework, and hospitals have limited ability to steer activity.

reforms.statement: The quadripartite committee adopted proposed efficiency measures expected to save or raise EUR 95 million in total, reached gradually; those with the largest financial impact concern medicines, medical cost control (maîtrise médicalisée), hospital care and action against abuse and fraud.

A government bill would bring 'ambulatory care structures', which associations or companies of doctors could run, under the hospital law to provide dialysis, non-surgical day hospitalisation, oncology and some minor procedures in ophthalmology, dermatology, abdominal-wall and proctological surgery, and urology.

locator.section: Un cadre légal pour les structures ambulatoires de soins

reforms.statement: Under the bill each ambulatory care structure would need an operating licence from the minister and an agreement with a hospital covering patient referral, transfer and access to hospital resources.

locator.section: Qualité, sécurité et continuité des soins

reforms.statement: On 29 April 2026 two deputies tabled a bill to create a right to universal health care coverage and amend the Social Security Code.

The bill would also remove the three-month waiting period that CUSS beneficiaries face because they are enrolled as voluntary insured, even though the State pays their contributions and care from day one.

locator.section: Exposé des motifs: Projet pilote de la CUSS

reforms.statement: Luxembourg has no national agency for medicines and health products; in January 2025 the government submitted revised legislation to create one.
In July 2024 breast cancer screening was widened to women aged 45-74 (previously 50-70), and the starting age for colorectal screening was lowered to 45.
A master's degree in medicine to follow the bachelor's programme is under discussion; if an evaluation due by the end of 2025 is favourable, it could start in 2027.

Between 2024 and 2026 the National Health Observatory, with OECD and European Commission support, developed a national health system performance assessment framework with over 30 stakeholders: 12 domains, 30 subdomains and 105 indicators.
Luxembourg's first National Health Plan, published in 2023, sets policy directions for population health, care pathways and the system's operating framework, but without measurable objectives so far.
